title: The Romance of the Forest, Interspersed with Some Pieces of Poetry. In Three Volumes
description: The third novel of Ann Radcliffe and the first great popular success of the Gothic romance of terror, published anonymously in three volumes on 22 December 1791 as the work of the authoress of A Sicilian Romance. Adeline, an orphaned girl of secretly noble fortune, is handed over by her father's appointment to the guardianship of her unscrupulous kinsman the Marquis de Montalt, who schemes to marry her and seize her inheritance. Driven from her home with the family of Pierre de La Motte, her guardian's steward, she takes refuge in a ruined forest abbey, where she discovers old manuscripts recording a tragic captivity of the seventeenth century, and passes through a series of shelters and imprisonments, at the chateau of La Motte and in the castle of La Valombrosa, before her parentage is cleared, her pursuer defeated, and her hand won by the soldier Theodore. The abbey papers and the slow documentary unveiling set the pattern Radcliffe perfected in The Mysteries of Udolpho, and the interspersed songs and ballads mark the place of her romance in the lyricised Gothic.
plot_or_argument: Adeline, born into wealth but kept by her father's quarrel from her claim, is educated in a convent and placed under the Marquis de Montalt, whose proposals she refuses. The La Motte family, Pierre, his wife Theresa and their children, befriend and shelter her; her flight with them leads to the ruined abbey, where she reads the manuscripts of a hermit's tragic past; she is pursued by Montalt's agents, falls under the power of interested priests at La Valombrosa, and is separated from Theodore, the young officer she loves, who is imprisoned for defending her. Forgeries, murders and a stolen heiress are at last laid open; the family that betrayed her is punished and broken, Adeline is restored to her fortune and rank, and after mourning her father she marries Theodore.
narrative_structure: A continuous prose romance in three volumes centred on Adeline's successive protection and expulsion, punctuated by embedded documents: the abbey manuscripts, recovered papers and a final expository revelation that explains by natural and legal causes what the scenery had clothed in terror.
principal_characters: Adeline, the orphaned heiress; the Marquis de Montalt, her grasping kinsman; Pierre de La Motte and his wife Theresa; their children; Theodore, the soldier whom Adeline loves; Arnaud La Luc, the exile and his family; Jerome, the forest hermit; Theresa and the abbey manuscripts
literary_form: Gothic novel and romance of terror; sentimental fiction of the pursued heroine with interspersed songs and ballads and embedded manuscript narrative
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose romance; the interspersed pieces of poetry are short lyric songs and ballads, hymns of the cloister and of the forest hermitage, set into the mouths of characters and subordinate to the prose.
historical_context: Published two years after A Sicilian Romance had begun Radcliffe's career and in the first years of the war with Revolutionary France, when debates over tyranny, property and providence made the abused heiress and the crooked guardian powerful political emblems; it appeared in the three-volume duodecimo format of the circulating libraries, at the height of the vogue for monastic ruins and picturesque scenery fostered by Gilpin and by the antiquarian revival of Gothic.
literary_significance: The Romance of the Forest made Radcliffe the most read English novelist of the 1790s and fixed the working formula of the Gothic romance: the persecuted heroine, the ruin as refuge, the hidden archive, and detection explained by natural causes. It shaped Gothic fiction through Mary Shelley and the Victorian sensation novel, provoked the parody that Jane Austen gave the genre in Northanger Abbey, and established the model of terror regulated by sensibility and reason.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as by the authoress of A Sicilian Romance; the authorship of Ann Radcliffe is undisputed, established by the designations of the successive editions and by her husband's memoir of 1826.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 22 December 1791, in three volumes, for T. Hookham and J. Carpenter, as stated by Chris Murray, Ann Radcliffe, Romanticism and the Gothic (Cambridge University Press, 2017) and by the article The Romance of the Forest in the Encyclopaedia Britannica-line Wikipedia account; the second edition of 1792 was issued by the same houses; the standard modern text is the Oxford World's Classics edition edited by Chloe Chard, cited in the bibliographies of Mary Ellen Snodgrass, Encyclopedia of Gothic Literature, and of Romantic Fiction and Literary Excess in the Minerva Press Era.

title: The Mysteries of Udolpho. A Romance; and Interspersed with Some Pieces of Poetry. In Four Volumes
description: The fourth novel of Ann Radcliffe, published in four volumes in May 1794 under her own name, and the masterwork of the Gothic romance of terror. Emily St. Aubert, educated in the Languedoc chateau of Le Blanc by a father whose death on a Pyrenean journey is softened by a monastery funeral and the mourned abbey of St. Clare, falls in love with Valancourt against her aunt Madame Cheron's will; her aunt's runaway second marriage to the Italian Signor Montoni carries Emily into the Apennines and into the castle of Udolpho, where Montoni tyrannises over her person and her hopes of an inheritance. A labyrinth of Italian strongholds follows, of subterranean passages and intercepted letters, of the veiled figure that proves a wax image, of the death of the Signora Montoni and the terrors of banditti, until the mysterious papers, the miniature of the Marchioness de Villeroi found in her father's closet, and the confession of a dying nun make known an old tragedy of enforced vows and jealousy; Emily recovers her fortune, and her constancy is rewarded by the reconciliation of Valancourt.
plot_or_argument: Emily's father St. Aubert dies on the way from the Pyrenees; under her aunt Madame Cheron she is forced into the society of the usurping Montoni, who seizes the castle of Udolpho and would coerce her into signing away her hopes and into a match with a wealthy Italian count; her lover Valancourt, already dismissed by St. Aubert for supposed dissipation, is absent and tried by his own errors. Emily escapes through the castle's secret ways, falls among banditti, is befriended by honest Italians and by the family of Villefort, endures the mysteries of the covered figure, the poisoned draughts and the lady of the papers, and hears at last the Marchioness de Villeroi's whole story: Montoni's imprisonment in the Venetian states and his death leave her wealthy, and her tried love is restored.
narrative_structure: A continuous four-volume romance following a single heroine's experience from the Pyrenees to the Apennines and back toward France, sustained by embedded papers, songs and a concluding expository narrative that resolves every appearance of the supernatural into natural and juridical causes.
principal_characters: Emily St. Aubert; St. Aubert, her father; Madame Cheron, her aunt, later Signora Montoni; the Marchioness de Villeroi, lost to the family history; Valancourt, Emily's lover; Signor Montoni; the Signora Montoni; the Count de Villefort and the Marchioness's story in the papers; Madame Montoni's attendant Annette; Sister St. Agnes of the convent; Du Pont and his brother the Abbot of St. Clare
literary_form: Gothic novel and romance of terror, the exemplary form of the explained supernatural, with interspersed songs and pastorals
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose romance; the interspersed poetry is lyric - songs, pastorals and the Castellan's air, Emily's own verses and the monk's hymn - in regular stanzas, with the great descriptive passages of mountain and lake scenery carrying a poetry of the picturesque within the prose.
historical_context: Published in 1794, in the war with Revolutionary France and the height of the Italian picturesque bred of travel and of Ann Radcliffe's own tours, and the year of her Lake District journey; issued in four volumes by G.G. and J. Robinson as by Ann Radcliffe, it was the first of her novels to carry her name, and its success made the sale of her next copyright one of the largest paid a woman writer of the age.
literary_significance: The Mysteries of Udolpho is the most famous and most imitated of English Gothic novels, the book by which the literature of terror became the dominant prose mode of the 1790s: it defined the pursued-heroine plot, castle and convent scenery, and the ethics of terror regulated by explanation; it was read, praised and parodied across the century, with Catherine Morland's raptures in Northanger Abbey measuring Austen's generation against it, and it remained in print into the Oxford World's Classics and Norton Critical editions.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's own name, Ann Radcliffe; authorship undisputed. The later prefaces and the Memoir of 1826 document its place as the decisive success of her career.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1794, in four volumes, by G.G. and J. Robinson, on 8 May 1794, as recorded by the article The Mysteries of Udolpho (citing the first-edition copy) and confirmed by the four-volume first edition of 1794 printed by G.G. and J. Robinson held in the Jane Austen's House collection; the Marchioness de Villeroi's relationship to St. Aubert is verified from the text in the Toronto Metropolitan University open pressbook edition; modern scholarly editions include the Oxford World's Classics text edited by Rictor Norton and the Norton Critical Edition.

title: The Italian, or, The Confessional of the Black Penitents. A Romance. In Three Volumes
alternative_titles: The Confessional of the Black Penitents
description: The last prose romance of Ann Radcliffe, advertised in the London press in December 1796 and published in three volumes with the imprint of 1797, of which she sold the copyright to Thomas Cadell. Vincentio di Vivaldi, seeing Ellena di Rosalba at church in Naples, loves her at first sight against the pride of his family; Ellena, reared in seclusion on the coast of Sorrento, is carried off on the road by the robbers who own Schedoni for their chief, is driven through the caverns of the banditti and the fortress of the suitorous Duke of Braccivalo, is accused of a murder committed in her chamber by Schedoni's assassin Spalatro, and is pressed by ecclesiastical arts into vows, while the confessional of the black penitents and the Inquisition darken the way. The disclosures at the close unite the houses of Schedoni and Ellena, establish her nobility so that Vivaldi may honourably wed her, and unbind the terrible history of the Schedoni family from which the title-piece takes its name.
plot_or_argument: Ellena, beloved of Vivaldi, is kidnapped on the road to Naples by robbers under Schedoni, protected from harm by his own troubled conscience, and pursued by the suit of the powerful Duke of Braccivalo, whom her pride and her lover's danger oblige her to resist; a murder in her lodging, done by the assassin Spalatro, throws suspicion on herself, and she is driven toward the convent and its arts of the confessional to escape forced marriage. Schedoni's history, of anhouse disowned, a sister lost, and the black-robed penitents of his family's Easter rite, is unfolded till he finds in Ellena a kinswoman, her parentage is cleared, the crimes are brought home to their authors, and her marriage with Vivaldi is made lawful in honour.
narrative_structure: A continuous three-volume romance, close-knit and rapid beside its predecessors, moving through abduction, pursuit, accusation and trial toward a single expository revelation that ties the robbers' chief to the heroine's house and resolves the machinery of the confessional and the Inquisition.
principal_characters: Ellena di Rosalba; Vincentio di Vivaldi; Schedoni, captain of the robbers; Spalatro, his assassin; the Duke of Braccivalo; Vivaldi's mother; Ellena's father; the sister and confessor of the Schedoni house; the Inquisition of Naples
literary_form: Gothic novel and romance of terror, with the confessional, the robbers' cavern and the Inquisition for its machinery; the last of the mature prose romances Radcliffe published in her lifetime
meter_and_prosody: Prose romance without interspersed verse; the rhythm of the book is that of its tragic scene-setting, the bay of Sorrento, the caverns and the fortress, and its style is nearer to tragedy than to the lyricism of Udolpho.
historical_context: Published at the close of the first vogue of the Gothic, when the campaign against the Inquisition and monastic craft was a staple of radical as well as Tory polemic, and when the Directory's wars had made Italy a subject of anxious English attention; its December 1796 press notice and the Cadell copyright mark the height of Radcliffe's fame before her withdrawal from publication.
literary_significance: The Italian is by many judges Radcliffe's most accomplished romance, concentrating her method into a single tragic fable of conscience and persecution; it stood as the school-example of the explained supernatural and of Gothic's anti-clerical machinery through the nineteenth century, was a measure for Scott's and Peacock's accounts of terror, and remains the canonical companion volume to Udolpho in the Gothic syllabus.
attribution_notes: Published as by the author of The Mysteries of Udolpho on the title page; the newspapers of December 1796 name Ann Radcliffe, and her authorship is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1797, in three volumes, duodecimo, printed for T. Cadell junior and W. Davies (successors to Mr. Cadell), the imprint and three-volume format confirmed by the auction descriptions of the first edition (Swann Galleries and the Darabanth/onebid catalogue entries transcribing the title page) and by the December 1796 advertisement quoted in the article The Italian (Radcliffe novel); the standard modern scholarly editions are the Oxford World's Classics text edited by Frederick Garber and revised by Nick Groom (2017) and the Penguin edition edited by Robert Miles.

title: A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794, through Holland and along the Eastern Frontier of France; in a Series of Letters. With Observations on the Sublime and Beautiful, as They Appear in the Works of Nature, and the Arts
alternative_titles: A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794
A Journey through Holland and along the Eastern Frontier of France
description: Ann Radcliffe's book of travel, the record of the continental journey of the summer of 1794, written as the tour proceeded and published in 1795 under her own name. In a series of letters she keeps the road through Holland, along the Rhine and the eastern frontier of France, and by the way of Switzerland and the Netherlands, describing cities, ruins, mining countries and mountain scenery with the eye of the novelist of Udolpho, weighing the effect of landscape on the feeling mind, and appending remarks on the sublime and the beautiful and on picturesque beauty that bring her theory of Gothic scene-setting before the reader of fact. It is the only book of her own composition on travel, the companion to the romances that its scenery explains, and one of the Romantic period's documents of the woman tourist's eye.
plot_or_argument: No argument in the strict sense: the letters report the progress of the tour, the company kept, the towns and passes seen, with continuous observation of the effect of scenery, an account of a mining party near the Laerboom and Falck, an excursion up the Rhine, and reflections on the picturesque, on the conduct of tourists, and on the effect of great landscape on the mind; the closing remarks on the sublime and beautiful draw the aesthetic theory out of the journey.
narrative_structure: A tour in letter form, sequential by road and date, framed by general observations on taste and scenery; the design is associative rather than argumentative, with descriptive set-pieces and a final aesthetic essay.
principal_characters: the lady travellers and their party, including Radcliffe herself as observing narrator; guides, post-horses and country people met on the road
literary_form: Travel writing in a series of letters with appended aesthetic observations; topographical and descriptive prose
meter_and_prosody: Prose; no verse. The style is the measured descriptive manner of the picturesque writers, with the balanced sentence of aesthetic essay in the closing remarks.
historical_context: Written on the tour of the summer of 1794, the year of Udolpho's publication and of the war that made the Rhine and the frontier of France a theatre of campaign, and published in 1795 in the full tide of the picturesque vogue that Gilpin, the tour books and the Lake and Alpine journals had created; Radcliffe's own 1794 excursions, the Lakes tour of that summer and the continental journey here recorded, belonged to the married freedom she had won a few years before.
literary_significance: A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794 is the primary document of Radcliffe's aesthetics of landscape outside the fiction, the evidence by which her scenes of terror are read as picturesque science, and an early book-length example of a English woman's published tour; it remains the standard witness for the scenery of the Rhine and the eastern frontier in the revolutionary war years and for the theory of the sublime and beautiful current in Romantic prose.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name, Ann Radcliffe; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1795, printed for G.G. and J. Robinson, Paternoster-Row; the imprint and the single-volume 1795 edition are recorded by the British Travel Writing database of the University of Wolverhampton (which cites the copy collated x, 500 pp.) and by WorldCat records for the 1795 issue; a second edition of the same year followed; the tour is documented in the Cumbria and Chawton House studies of Radcliffe's travel.

title: Gaston de Blondeville; or, The Court of Henry the Third, Keeping Festival in Ardenne. A Romance; St. Alban's Abbey, a Metrical Tale; with Some Poetical Pieces
alternative_titles: St. Alban's Abbey, a Metrical Tale
description: The posthumous collection that closed Ann Radcliffe's printed career, issued in four volumes by Henry Colburn in 1826, three years after her death, and prefixed with the Memoir of the Author with Extracts from her Journals, the first life of her, edited from her papers by her husband. It contains Gaston de Blondeville, her historical romance of the court of Henry III of England keeping festival in Ardenne, left as a large fragment, and St. Alban's Abbey, a metrical tale in the antique mould, with other poetical pieces. The volume is the chief witness of her later temper: the romances of the 1790s abandoned, the picturesque journals and the ballad and metrical tale preferred, and the whole career surveyed by the Memoir that made her literary testament public.
plot_or_argument: Gaston de Blondeville, in its unfinished sweep, brings together the Saxon and Norman factions, the outlaws of the forest and the court festival of Henry III in Ardenne, tracing Gaston's fortunes, the love of Matilda of Dinant, the tyranny of the house of Mountfort and the forest legend of the fatal assembly; St. Alban's Abbey, in verse, tells the tale of Edwy, of the abbey and of the lost heiress of the house of Walderie, the metrical descendant of her own prose romances; the Memoir prefixed records the life, the retirement from publication, the journals of tour, and the death of the authoress.
narrative_structure: A posthumous miscellany: the romance fragment, the metrical tale and shorter poems gathered after the author's death and presented with a prose Memoir compiled from her journals and papers by her husband; the parts are independent, unified by the life that frames them.
principal_characters: Gaston de Blondeville; Matilda of Dinant; the Saxon Outlaw of the Woods; the house of Mountfort and the court of Henry III; in St. Alban's Abbey, Edwy and the outcast of Walderie; Ann Radcliffe herself as the subject of the Memoir
literary_form: Posthumous fragmentary historical romance, metrical tale and shorter verse, with a prose memoir compiled from journals
meter_and_prosody: The metrical tale is in the antique romantic stanza and measure of the ballad and the old romance, deliberate in its archaism; the fragment of Gaston is in prose of historical elevation; the Memoir is plain domestic prose.
historical_context: Published in 1826 to a literary scene remade by Scott's historical novel, of which Radcliffe's Ardenne romance is an unconscious antecedent; the Memoir and journals were the husband's disposal of her papers after her death in February 1823, answering a public that had known nothing from her in prose fiction since The Italian in 1797.
literary_significance: Gaston de Blondeville with its Memoir is the foundation document of Radcliffe's biography and reception, the source of nearly all knowledge of her life and character, and the record of her post-1797 imaginative writing; the metrical tale and the fragment are the evidence of the Gothic novelist's turn to romance in the antique and to verse at the close of her career, and the volume's account of her journals anchors the study of her travel writing.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name, the posthumous authorship of the romances and metrical tale by Ann Radcliffe established by the Memoir of her husband; the Memoir itself is compiled by William Radcliffe from her journals and papers and is not by her hand.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1826, in four volumes, Henry Colburn, New Burlington Street, with the prefixed Memoir of the Author with Extracts from her Journals; the title and volumes confirmed by the HathiTrust catalogue record and by the digitised copy at the University of Illinois Library which prints the Colburn imprint; St. Alban's Abbey and the poetical pieces are bound up with the romance as the half-title states.
